election-day-richmond-1880-11-02.A7:
Those Emissaries.
F. C. LOVELAND and F. A. BURR were the Radical emissaries from the North who were relied upon by the high contracting parties to make such an alliance between the Mabonites and the Republicans as would secure the defeat of all the Democratic candidates for Congress. Here is one of their documents:

[From the Baltimore American, 3d.]

VOTERS DISFRANCHISED IN VIRGINIA.—The following was received at the Republican national headquarters to-day:

“RICHMOND, VA., November 2, 1880.

“To Hon. M. Jewell:

“Under pretence of an injunction issued by a little corporation judge out of Richmond, judges of election are throwing out all tax-receipts signed by collectors appointed by the Auditor. They have already thrown out from 400 to 600. Think we may still pull through, unless this infamy injures us more than is expected. This is the last desperate attempt of the Bourbons to save themselves from an overwhelming defeat.

F. C. LOVELAND,

“F. A. BURR.”

That’s rich. It shows how much Messrs. BURR and LOVELAND knew about the state of parties and the feeling of the voters in this State. They have lost all reputation. They are neither diplomats nor fit parties to be entrusted with the duty of making a political diagnosis. We would say, “Let BURR and LOVELAND retire,” but that we take it for granted that they have departed these coasts. Their libel upon Judge Clopton will only cause a smile of derision to wrinkle the face of the Judge. They are not worthy to unloose the latchets of his shoes.

LETTERS FROM THE PEOPLE.
DFMOCRATIC METHODS IN VIRGINIA.
DEMOCRATIC METHODS IN VIRGINIA.
HOW THE STATE WAS CARRIED FOR HANCOCK—GROSS PERVERSIONS OF LAW BY DEMOCRATIC OFFICIALS.
To the Editor of The Tribune.

SIR: Permit me to call your attention to some facts connected with the recent campaign and election in the Metropolitan District of this State, in which three Congressional candidates were placed in the field, namely: George D. Wise, Bourbon; John S. Wise, Readjuster Democrat; and H. L. Pelouse, Republican, who finally withdrew in favor of John S. Wise.

The law of this State provides that voters must be duly registered, and must have paid $1 poll tax previous to the day of election. This tax is to be paid to the clerk of the court of the city or county in which the voter resides. Accordingly the colored men flocked to the clerk's office of the Hustings Court, to Andrew Jenkins, clerk, who is a known Democratic partisan. There they met their first repulse, being told to go to the City Treasurer, who would immediately make out a tax bill for the city and collect their money. Hundreds were fooled in this way until their friends told them better, when the clerk's office was again besieged by an eager crowd, where all possible detentions and annoyances were placed in their way. Many were told that they were not assessed, others that they had already paid, and others that their names were not on the books. Thus a thousand men were cheated and defrauded, while others became disheartened and would not apply.

John E. Massey, State Auditor, seeing these things, applied the lawful remedy and appointed as tax collector William H. Beveridge, now a member of the Readjuster party, who had formerly been a leader of the Bourbon Democracy. Then the Bourbons, finding that their plan had failed and that many colored men were going to his office and paying the tax, met in secret conclave to conspire against him. On Sunday night his office was attacked, his signs torn down, and his office otherwise mutilated. Yet he held the fort, and did his duty like a man. The Bourbons then proceeded to the Courts to try some legal process to stop Mr. Beveridge from receiving the tax. They applied to all the city judges for an injunction but were refused. Then they applied to a judge of an adjourning county, a scissored partisan, who granted their prayer. This injunction was served on Mr. Beveridge at nightfall, when relief could not be had from the Courts; the Bourbon judges or elec-
applied to a joke, who granted their prayer. This injunction was served on Mr. Beveridge at nightfall, when distress could not be had from the Courts; the Bourbon judges of election were notified not to receive his receipts, and thus thousands of voters were turned from the polls. Not only in Richmond but all through the State it is now an ascertained fact that more than enough men were thus denied the right of suffrage to have cast the electoral vote of the State for the Republican candidate.

But the outrage did not stop here. At the polls exconvicts, blacklegs, Ku-Klimx and others were stationed, who threatened the negroes with the penitentiary and with mob law; their tax receipts were taken from them and torn up, and they handover to the police as illegal voters, detained until sundown, and then released. too late to vote. This is the Soud South; this is the land of freedom.

Richmond, Va, Nov. 5, 1830.

John Wise "Speaks a Piece." [1995] 1000.
[For the Dispatch.]
To My Supporters for Congress:

Fellow Citizens,—I am daily asked the question whether I will contest for the seat in Congress from this district, and I feel it to be a duty I owe to you as well as to myself to make a public statement on the subject. When I became a candidate for Congress I promised to do all in my power to succeed. That promise has certainly been redeemed. No man ever worked more earnestly and unceasingly than did I to achieve success. I believe I am right, I believe our cause is right. I have done nothing I am sorry for, nothing I am ashamed of, and am as ready to renew the fight when occasion occurs as if I had been triumphantly elected. The returns are against us by a large majority. With opinions and convictions unchanged, I accept the result without a murmur. Regrets I have—not regrets for the lost bauble of personal success, but that our party has not been triumphant in this fight. Its ultimate supremacy I regard as certain, but I regret that the battle must be fought again, whereas a victory for us in the last contest would have ended strife.

I will not contest my opponent's return. The wish that I should do so is freely indulged by many of our friends. If I could do so conscientiously I would not hesitate an instant. I would owe it as a duty to my supporters, no matter what the cost or trouble, and I feel certain they have confidence in my fidelity to them sufficient to assure them I would not fail to make the contest if I had a case.

However sperate ardent supporters may be they must remember I am as much interested as they are, and have perhaps better information than any one else as to the facts.

Immediately after the election I canvassed the district by precincts, addressing a letter to one or more trusted friends in every voting-precinct to ascertain all frauds and similar influences, and the extent thereof. Also to ascertain the effect of the injunction issued by the Judge of Manchester. I have received replies in detail from nearly every precinct in the district, and am fully informed now upon these points.

The returned majority of my opponent is 2,365. Undoubtedly I lost about 1,300 votes in the district by the action of Judge William Izard Clopton, granting an injunction restraining the judges of election from receiving the votes of parties holding tax-receipts from collectors, and by the partisan course of Funder judges of election who, although not enjoined, took their cue from him and refused such votes. I forbear from any expression of my opinion of the conduct or motives of the judge who issued that process. Perhaps I could not give an impartial opinion. As to the law justifying it, no reputable lawyer would damage his reputation by arguing in favor of the proposition. I am advised that Judge Fitzhugh, to whom the bill was addressed, and perhaps others, declined to grant the injunction. It may be, however, that Judge William Izard Clopton, during the intervals between his excited political speeches in behalf of my competitor, learned some law, unknown to the calm and wise Fitzhugh, authorizing and justifying the issuing of an injunction without notice, served at sundown, the day before election, which virtually dis-franchised 1,300 legal voters without opportunity or hope of recess. In a contest for these excluded votes I entertain no doubt I would have them counted for me.

Friends have urged that I contest for them, and claim that the moral effect of their exclusion and the intimidation produced by the injunction and several absurd manifestoes preceding and following it was such that the election was not a fair expression of the popular will of the district. The logic of this is that by these things I lost not only these 1,300 votes, but 1,065 other voters of people who would otherwise have voted for me.

I am not, as at present advised, prepared to take this ground in a petition, and thereby to declare my solemn belief of the truth of the assertion.

I have been unable to ascertain that such was the effect of this injunction in the counties; much less am I prepared to sustain the position by proofs. My observation of its effect in Richmond was that several gentlemen known to me, filled with the disgust and contempt which greeted the injunction here, refused to vote, whereas otherwise they would have voted against me. I have been unable to learn the names of any persons not holders of tax-collectors' receipts who were deterred by the injunction from voting for me.

As to the count of votes actually cast in Richmond, I believe it was the fairest count ever made in this city. I took such precautions as to make cheating in the count here next to impossible.

Frauds to a small extent were practiced at several precincts in the country. At a precinct in Chesterfield and one in Hanover the registration books were mutilated so as to exclude colored voters, but the extent of these was insignificant, amounting only to about 20 or 30 at each.

Treats of discharge from service for voting for me were indulged in at Ashland and elsewhere. These belong to the grand jury of the Federal court, if anywhere, and I have nothing to do with them.

Whiskey and money were undoubtedly freely used in various sections against me—by whom furnished I know not and care not.

Undoubtedly no election for years in this district has been productive of more campaign falsehoods, more active canvassing, more insidious and injurious but intangible frauds, than were resorted to to mislead the people and secure my defeat.

These things, while known of all men amongst us, are, however, not susceptible of proof in any form that would be available. It is the lot of every man who enters upon political life, and I do not complain.

The three great causes of my defeat were:

Judge William Izard Clopton's injunction.

The utter paucity of the Readjuster vote in the city of Richmond.

The active opposition of General Williams C. Wickham and his son.

As to the first, I have spoken.

As to the second, I confess my surprise. We calculated upon a vote of 1,500 for the July ticket in Richmond. We received only about 400. As to why we received no more it is unnecessary to discuss. If we had received what we expected I would have been elected in spite of the Wickham influence. I ran ahead of the combined Readjuster and Republican vote in Richmond. My competitor ran behind his ticket in the city. It was, therefore, owing to no fault of mine.

As to the opposition of the Wickhams to me I have no complaint to make. They had a perfect right to vote and work for whom

VIRGINIA REPUBLICANS DISFRANCHISED.
RICHMOND Dec 2 R.B. Foster James Gale
RICHMOND, Dec. 2.—R. B. Foster, James Galloway and Samuel Logan, judges of election in Manchester, have been arrested for refusing to receive the votes of colored men on election day. These votes were rejected because the parties did not show, as it is alleged, proper capitation tax receipts. The case is before United States Commissioner Atkins.
election-day-richmond-1880-11-02.A14:
HOW THE TAX COLLECTORS WERE APPOINTED AND DISCHARGED—THEIR DUTY IN THE FREE STATE—ELECTION JUDGES BROUGHT TO CONDIGN—HOW THE AVERAGE VOTER OVER THE RIVER SECURED HIS TAX-RECEIPT WITHOUT PAYING FOR IT—KIND FRIENDS WHO PUT UP THE SPONDULIX, &c. &c.

The cases of R. B. Foster, James Galloway, and Simuel Logan, judges at the late election in the Third Ward, Manchester, charged with "unlawfully refusing or omitting to receive, count, certify, register, report, or give effect to the votes of Edmund Field, John Burton, George Jefferson, James Thompson, James T. Thompson, Jr., C. W. Jones, Nelson Crump, Melvin Hill, G. C. Washington, W. H. Smith, Moses Dennis, S. E. Woodson, Richard Crump, and W. H. Anderson, upon their offer to vote, they then and there being duly qualified voters in the Third-Ward precinct, Manchester"—or, in other words, charged with refusing to allow them to vote at the late election upon tax-receipts issued from the office of the Auditor of Public Accounts of Virgnia—came up before United States Commissioner Aikins yesterday morning.

Quite a number of persons were present at the examination, most of whom were summoned as witnesses. Several hours were spent in hearing the testimony, and some interesting facts, showing how the election business was carried on in the "free State" by the "faithful allies" were brought out. The parties accused were repre-ented by Hon. George D. Wise and A. M. Keiley, Esq., and the prosecution was conducted by United States District-Attorney L. L. Lewis.

EXAMINATION OF WITNESSES.

Richard Crump, the first witness examined, said he tried to vote in the Third Ward, but his vote was not received. He did not know why. Nothing was said; they only handed him back his receipt and told him to stand aside. Mr. Redford and Page told him he could not vote. They said he could not vote without his receipt. He did not know whether they challenged his vote or not.

James T. Thompson, another colored witness, said he tried to vote in the Third Ward, but could not. He handed in his receipt, and it was handed back to him. Simuel Logan and another gentleman were the judges. Some of the judges challenged his vote; he did not know who. He heard some one say, "I challenge that vote." He didn't know on what grounds they refused the vote.

Mr. Keiley: Didn't you inquire.

Witness: I asked some of the bystanders to tell me, but they did not. I said nothing to the judges. I think the challenger was inside. The tax-receipt was passed back to M. A. Harris and he handed it to me.

SUPERVISOR'S TESTIMONY.

M. A. Harris (also colored) was the next witness examined. He had acted as supervisor on the day of election. He was at the polls all day. The witness read a list of voters whose votes were rejected. He said Richard Crump came to the polls and offered to vote, and was rejected on the ground that he had paid his taxes to one of the clerks of the Auditor. In the beginning there had been a contest, the witness said, as to who were the authorized parties to collect delinquent taxes. Some contended that Mr. George W. Duesberry had no authority to receipt for the taxes. Witness said he addressed a note to Auditor Massey making the inquiry as to the matter, and received the following in reply:

“COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA,
“OFFICE OF THE
“AUDITOR OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS,
“RICHMOND, November 2, 1880.

“G. W. Duesberry, William R. Smith, R. A. Noel, John R. Miller, James A. Seddon, and W. W. Massey are authorized to receipt for all payments with the State Treasury, including delinquent and insolvent capitation-taxes.

“W. N. NEWMAN,
“Clerk of Accounts.”

The judges, however, held that that paper did not entitle them to vote.

THE LETTER.

Question: What did the judges say when you showed that letter from the Auditor's office? Answer: They said that did not amount to anything. I claimed that this man did have a right to vote. Mr. Logan was somewhat in sympathy with them, and he claimed that the parties ought to vote, but the other two judges decided otherwise.

James Thompson, Jr., also produced his receipt. “There was a vast crowd around the polls, and I thought Mr. Page and Mr. Redford were acting very disorderly. It was quite difficult for any one to get up to the polls to vote.”

Q. How many voters were rejected on that day on the ground that these tax-receipts were not proper? A. Thirteen.

Q. Was that the only ground upon which they were rejected? A. Yes, sir. I insisted upon the right of all those present to vote. I sent over to Auditor Massey, and his chief clerk sent me that communication, stating that they were authorized. [The witness went on to say that the judges in the Fourth Ward had addressed a communication to Judge Clopton as to what they should do, and they were acting under the letter they received in reply.]

READJUSTER CHAIRMAN.

Mr. E. B. Howle (white) was the next witness. He said: I was chairman of the Reckojuster club, and was at the Third Ward a dozen times during the day. I saw votes refused there on the grounds that the tax-receipts were not valid. A man showed his office-receipt, signed by George W. Duesberry, and Mr. Foster refused to let him vote. I asked him by what authority, and he said he did not know whether Mr. Duesberry was a clerk under Massey or not. I said I was willing to swear that Duesberry was clerk in that office. I saw several votes rejected. I was offered the place of tax-collector for Manchester by the Auditor, but would not receive it. I expected there would be trouble of this kind, and would have nothing to do with it.

HOWLE REFUSES.

Q. How did you know those receipts were paid—did you have anything to do with paying them? A. I know they were all paid. I am willing to swear that they were all paid Friday, Saturday, or Monday before the election, and I refuse to answer if I had anything to do with paying for them. I refuse to answer that question.

Mr. Wise: We will put that down. Maybe we'll find some other things.

Mr. Kelley: Why do you refuse to answer that question, Mr. Howle?

RICHMOND, VA., Dec. 9.—The grand jury of the United States circuit court to-day indicted B. B. Foster, James F. Galloway and Samuel Logan, the latter colored, at Manchester, Va., judges of the election, for refusing the rights of suffrage to voters in the presidential election, who presented themselves to vote with capitation tax receipts, alleged to have been illegally issued from the state auditor's office. In answer to certain questions propounded to the court by the grand jury, before returning the indictment, Judge Hughes stated that the receipts, though not signed by the auditor in person, were legal, and that they had been legally issued. He further said that the judges of the election, while careful to see that the persons offering to vote are legally qualified voters, should disdain to act as obstructives to the progress of elections, which it is their duty to facilitate, and should rather be disposed to overlook mere technical difficulties than so to magnify them as to defeat a citizen to vote if he is meritoriously entitled to the right. He was further of the opinion that the grand jury, in passing upon such papers as the receipts in question, should act upon well settled and very necessary principles of law, and that official acts and the acts of public officers in the line of their official duty, must be presumed to have been rightly and legally done until the contrary is made to appear. So likewise judges of election not only have the right to act on this maxim but are bound to do so in discharge of their duty at the polls. They are sole judges, however, in all matters of doubt arising at the polls, and can not be interfered with at that time by any power of this state, whether executive or judicial.

VIRGINIA NEWS.
Charlottesville is to have a hook-and-ladder company.
Mr. James Kern, one of the oldest citizens of Winchester, is dead.
James Saunders, an old citizen of Norfolk, died from paralysis last week.
There are 1,300 men employed at the Tredegar Iron Works, in Richmond.
Sixteen Indians have arrived at Hampton, to be educated at the Normal High School.
Captain James F. Gibbs, of the steamer Breakwater, of the Old Dominion Line, is dead.
Granville Dawson, master of the sloop Wainwright, was drowned at Dutch Gap last Friday.
The District Grange of Northern Virginia will hold its next session in Alexandria on March 2.
A handsome sum has been raised at the University of Virginia in behalf of the Poe memorial fund.
Mr. Thomas H. Clagett, of the Loudoun bookstore, has been paralyzed and rendered speechless.
Mr. Samuel B. Witt has been appointed commonwealth attorney of Richmond, vice Hon. George D. Wise.
Ex-Governor James L. Kemper has been suffering from the effects of his wound received at Gettysburg.
The fruit growers of Clarke County say that the peach, plum, apricot, and cherry crops have been winter-killed.
At Williamson's last Friday a white barkeeper named Pugh shot and instantly killed a colored barber named Burrell.
The State Agricultural Society will hold a grand fair on the fair grounds near Richmond during the Yorktown Centennial.
Virginia members of Congress are sending large quantities of cotton-seed to the planters of the south-side counties of that State.
J. Q. Bass, a Henry County planter, sold 1,478 pounds of leaf tobacco in Danville a few days ago, at an average of $47 per hundred.
The Methodists at Leesburg are having a very spicy controversy over the ownership of certain property, said to belong to the church.
The Rev. William N. Ward, one of the oldest of the Episcopal clergy of Virginia, died at his home in Richmond County on Friday last.

Miss Alice Astrop, of Lee County, seventeen years of age, having been betrayed, committed suicide last week by drowning herself in the river.

In the United States court at Richmond the jury in the case of the indicted judges of election in Manchester failed to agree and were discharged.

It is said the counsel for the trustees in the Atlantic, Mississippi, and Ohio Railroad case will receive a fee of $75,000, and the master of the court $10,000.

The rush of freight at Norfolk is reported to be greater than has been known for years, the rows of trucks waiting to deliver goods extending at times for two miles.

General Roger A. Pryor has accepted the invitation from the literary societies of Richmond College to deliver the address at their celebration at the close of the session.

The quantity of iron-ore arriving at Lynchburg for shipment per the Virginia Midland Railroad is now so great that it is impossible to provide the necessary transportation for it.

The wife of Wilson Fowlkes (colored) has been sentenced to be hanged in Lunenburg County, Virginia, for murdering her husband. She brained him with an axe while he was asleep.

John Williamson, janitor of the courthouse at Petersburg, has been arrested, charged with the theft of a number of canceled coupon bonds, amounting to about $4,000, stolen from the auditor's office.

The big "porker," bred and owned by Mr. James Dugan, of Berkeley County, is the largest hog in the United States, and is a real curiosity. It will weigh 1,200 pounds, and is about the size of an Alderney cow.

Frank Trigg, jr., a worthy and intelligent colored man, has been appointed principal of the Polk-street colored school, at Lynchburg, to succeed Miss Fanny Harvey (white), who has been promoted to the Jackson street school.

A Negro Fiend Swung to a Telegraph Pole.

A Negro Fiend Swung to a Telegraph Pole.
Special to Little Rock Gazette.]

PINE BLUFF, December 4.—This morning at six o'clock a negro fiend entered the back door of Mr. Joe Miller's house. Mr. Miller is a butcher, and had left the premises, leaving the door unlocked. His wife and two children were in bed asleep. The fiend seized Mrs. Miller, who is a most estimable lady, and threw her on the floor, and succeeded, after almost choking her to death, in ravishing her.

Accomplishing his hellish purpose, he left the unconscious woman on the floor and, going to the wardrobe, took what money there was in it, which was one twenty and one three-dollar piece of gold, and some jewelry, and left.

When the news was spread, the people generally felt highly indignant and the telegraph was freely used and every search made. The fiend took the train for Arkansas City this morning, and was arrested there, bound in irons, and at this moment, three p.m., is on his way back to this place strongly guarded.

There is no telling what his fate may be. Mrs. Miller has just awhile ago been partially restored to consciousness.

LATER—7:30 p.m.—When the train arrived the prisoner was taken charge of and conducted to the bedside of Mrs. Miller, who, being perfectly conscious, recognized him. The family jewelry and the three-dollar piece of gold which was taken from his person, were also recognized and identified by all of the family. The negro's name is James Anderson. He was taken by force from the officers and carried in front of the courthouse and hung on a telegraph pole.

PINE BLUFF, Dec. 5.—A negro fiend named James Anderson entered the back door of Mr. James Miller's house at 6 o'clock this morning, and finding Mrs. Miller and her two children in bed, he seized the wife and after almost choking her to death, succeeded in ravishing her. Last Saturday morning a negro named James Anderson entered the house of Mr. Joseph Miller, in the casten suburb of Pine Bluff, ravished Mrs. Miller, and stole from a wardrobe in the house a sum of money and some articles of jewelry. Though search was made so soon as the alarm could be given the fellow succeeded in boarding the train for Arkansas City, which leaves about 7 o'clock, and but for Sheriff Bankston, of Desha county, who heard of the affair at Walnut Lake, would probably have escaped. But Bankston knew Jim as an old offender, and, seeing him on the train, questioned him as to where he was going, whither he had come, and so on, ending by arresting him on suspicion. The suspicion proved well grounded, and the prisoner was taken to Arkansas City and thence returned to Pine Bluff. While the train was on its way from Walnut Lake to Arkansas City, Anderson eluded the guard and jumped from the platform to the ground, giving leg-bail to the best of his ability. A colored brakeman saw the leap for liberty, caught the bell-rope, set up a brake and started in pursuit of the fugitive. The prisoner had several hundred yards the start, but the legs of the brakeman were the flectest, and he overhauled Anderson after a race of nearly half a mile and returned him to the custody of the guard on board the train. As the train approached Pine Bluff, Saturday evening, the engineer was flagged, a halt made, and a committee of ten prominent citizens of Jefferson county took the prisoner from the baggage-car, placed him on the engine, and requested the engineer to detach the locomotive from the train and convey the party and prisoner into town. The request was complied with, and, after being taken before Mrs. Miller and identified, Anderson was conveyed up town to Barraque street, and on a telegraph pole in front of the court house expiated his atrocious crime. He refused to confess or make any statement, his only ejaculation being, "Lord, have mercy!" as he was about to be hauled up. The execution was conducted in an orderly manner, and the entire population, white and black, expressed

Louis J. Jennings, in his London letter to the New York World, says that Beaconsfield's "Endymion," despite its faults, has taken the reading public of England by storm. There are plenty of critics, however, who point out the slip-shod writing, the bungling sentences, and the penny romance writer's touches of descriptions.

Amherst College has concluded that its students are men, their ages averaging 22, and will, therefore, no longer subject them to discipline as boys. They will hereafter be held responsible for their work, but not for their personal conduct, unless it interferes with their duties. This has long been the rule in German universities, but has never been fully tested in this country, though Harvard has, to a limited extent, adopted it.

While Mrs. Joseph Miller, of Pine Bluff, Ark., was alone, a negro named James Anderson entered her house, threw her on the floor, and, after nearly choking her to death, outraged her person. A resident of Baltimore has brought suit for $10,000 damages against the Western Union Telegraph Company for the death of his son, and another resident has brought suit against the same company for $2,000 for injuries to his son. The somewhat surprising grounds are that the company had left a telegraph pole unguarded on a truck in the public street, and these boys and others attempted to play 'see-saw upon it, and it toppled over, killing one of the boys and injuring the other.

The recent decline in coffee, of which this country uses more than any other nation in the world, and five times as much as Great Britain, will probably be permanent, as it is due, not to the casual over-supply, but to a change in the manner of conducting the trade. Railroads recently constructed from Rio Janeiro, bring the coffee more speedily from the plantations, and steamers, which have supplanted sailing vessels, have greatly shortened the trip from Brazil to this country. The trade in coffee, in other words, has gone through the same secular change as the trade in tea. The day for great firms buying by the ship-load and carrying great stocks has gone by. Orders by cable, shipments by steam and purchases by job lots have taken the place of the slow but princely methods of a few years back.

Captain J. H. Siddons, in some interesting personal reminiscences in the Washington Republic, records that the father of the late Duke of Cambridge had a habit of thinking aloud, and particularly manifested this singularity during the performance of divine service in the Protestant Episcopal Church. In the preliminary phrase from the pulpit, "Let us pray," he would add mutteringly and unconsciously, "by all means, very proper." He would respond to the commandment, "Thou shalt not steal," "certainly—very wrong to steal," and "Remember that thou keep holy the Sabbath day," received a commendatory response—"assuredly very right." It is recorded that on one occasion when "prayers for rain" were about to be offered up, he exclaimed, "No use—no use—the wind's easterly."

Lord Otho Fitzgerald, Lady Londesborough's second husband, appeared as one of the parties to the suit.
